☆ VideoTrail: Interactive Video Foraging Through Hierarchical Visualization
Catherine Yeh, Bryan Wang, Fernanda Viégas, Martin Wattenberg
People often watch videos to find information, but locating relevant moments can be difficult and time-consuming. Existing strategies like scrubbing rely primarily on visual scanning and linear search, providing limited support for goal-directed navigation. We present VideoTrail, an AI-powered browser extension that supports information seeking in videos through a hierarchical visualization. Inspired by information foraging theory, VideoTrail surfaces semantic and structural cues as information scent, creating an explorable roadmap of segments. The system is multimodal and adaptive, prioritizing visual or textual scent based on the video's content. In a user study (N=16), VideoTrail helped participants efficiently locate key moments and enabled new navigation strategies compared to traditional timelines, highlighting how exposing an adaptive video structure can enhance goal-directed viewing.
comment: 19 pages, 13 figures
♻ ☆ Déjà Cue: Localizing States in Object Histories via Vocabulary-Relative Coordinates
Haofan Cao, Zhichao You, Yunkai Yang, Liang Guo, Jie Wang, Chongshou Li
Object tracking preserves identity through visual changes, but cannot tell when an object is whole, cut, or peeled. We study state-moment retrieval: locating when a tracked object exhibits each state in a supplied set of descriptions. However, absolute image--text similarity can favor shared object semantics, obscuring the distinctions needed to localize individual states. Our insight is that the alternatives themselves provide a reference for measuring state evidence. We introduce Déjà Cue, a training-free framework that centers description embeddings on a state-balanced vocabulary mean, producing query directions that compare each state against its alternatives. Using frozen vision--language encoders, Déjà Cue calibrates frame scores and retrieves intervals at multiple durations within contiguous visible runs. We construct MS-VOST by annotating 620 object histories with 2,465 states. With the encoder and temporal search fixed, Déjà Cue improves all three localization metrics over absolute scoring across eight encoder configurations, raising Top-1 temporal IoU by 0.42--1.14 percentage points. These gains persist across four text constructions, and candidate-ranking analysis shows that the vocabulary reference brings relevant intervals forward within the same search space. These results establish the supplied state vocabulary as an object-specific reference for localizing semantic states from frozen visual representations.
comment: Code available at https://github.com/HaofanCao/DejaCue
♻ ☆ UEmo-D1: An Efficient and Calibrated Decision Model for Unified Multimodal Emotion Recognition
Daiqing Wu, Junqiao Wang, Chengyang Fang, Runhao Zeng, Fei Ma, Sicheng Zhao
Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) seeks to identify emotions conveyed through or elicited by media comprising diverse modality compositions. Research in this field has largely evolved along two paradigms: task-specific models and approaches based on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Despite their distinct strengths, neither fully reconciles three capabilities essential to human-like emotion understanding: cross-task generalization, efficient decision-making, and receptiveness to multiple plausible interpretations. Inspired by recent advances in decision models, we explore a unified framework that maps multimodal inputs, guided by natural language instructions, directly to distributions over candidate options, addressing these requirements through direct probabilistic decisions. We instantiate this framework in UEmo-D1, the first decision model for MER to our knowledge. To support joint training and systematic evaluation, we also curate UEmo-Data, comprising 977,270 training samples and 41 evaluation subsets across six MER tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate UEmo-D1's combination of strong recognition performance, low inference latency, and well-calibrated confidence estimates. Complementary analyses further reveal how training strategies and data composition influence these capabilities, providing practical insights into unified MER modeling. Together, our findings establish decision models as a feasible direction toward human-level emotion recognition. Project page: https://github.com/wdqqdw/UEmo-D1.

Information Retrieval
☆ LQ-Rec: Late Quantization for Sequential Recommendation
Satoshi Koide, Yueqi Wang, Julian McAuley
Generative retrieval (GR) for sequential recommendation compresses each item into a short semantic ID and trains an autoregressive decoder to generate next-item codes from a user history. While appealing for cold-start handling and storage, au- toregressive GR suffers a structural scaling limit: typically, longer semantic IDs reduce quantization error in principle but degrade ranking quality and quadratic memory usage against semantic ID length. We propose Late Quantization (LQ), a non-autoregressive paradigm that confines discretization to the output (item) side of the pipeline. The encoder and scoring rule operate in continuous space, while items are stored and matched as semantic IDs produced by an end-to-end-trained residual quantizer. This architectural shift permits an additive error decomposition and a pairwise ordering theorem that jointly bound the quantization- induced ranking drop, a structural guarantee absent in prior semantic-ID recommenders. Across four public benchmarks, the resulting recommender, LQ-Rec, delivers three capabilities simultaneously: ranking quality improves monotonically with the semantic-ID length and outperforms existing baselines; a single trained model supports anytime compression, tuning ranking quality against inference cost without retraining; and LQ-Rec shows superior generalization on a memorization/generalization partition.
☆ Retrieving Patristic References and Modelling Topics in Bullinger's Reformation Correspondence
Lena Pickartz, Philipp Schaer, Phillip B. Ströbel
The correspondence of Heinrich Bullinger (1504-1575), Swiss Reformer and Antistes of Zurich, documents the political and religious debates of the Reformation, including extensive appeals to the Church Fathers as authoritative sources. Detecting such references computationally remains largely unexplored. We investigate dense and sparse retrieval for patristic reference detection, and metadata-informed topic modelling as a proxy for the topics and ideas discussed. Prior work on Latin intertextuality has fine-tuned dense retrievers for their respective target domain, and we test how well these models transfer to Bullinger's correspondence. We compare lexical (BM25), dense (bi-encoders), and hybrid methods on explicit and implicit references. A Latin encoder fine-tuned on biblical reuse performs best among the bi-encoders (82%, Recall@20 on explicit and 16% on implicit references), while BM25 outperforms dense approaches on explicit citations (94%, R@20). Because BM25 and dense retrieval recover disjoint sets of implicit references, fusing their rankings raises implicit R@20 to 22%, close to cross-encoder reranking of the same candidates (26%) but without its inference cost. For topic modelling, we extend FASTopic with a seed-guided loss function and editorial abstract embeddings. Measurable coherence gains over the baseline remain minimal, but qualitative and temporal analysis shows that some topics track documented historical events. However, dominant topic weights barely exceed a uniform distribution, making topics unusable to inform retrieval. A pilot application of LLM-based concept induction (LLooM) further points towards a more human-interpretable alternative. Together, these results present a first approach to retrieving patristic references and modelling fine-grained topics in Bullinger's correspondence.
comment: Accepted for the Seventh Conference on Computational Humanities Research 2027. To be published in the Anthology of Computers and the Humanities
☆ LSP-RAG: Latent Scoring Perspectives for Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Haochen Liu, Guanghui Min, Song Wang, Yada Zhu, Chen Chen, Jundong Li
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in open-domain question answering, but often struggle with factual accuracy and multi-hop reasoning due to the incompleteness of the training corpora. A promising solution is Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (KG-RAG), which supplements LLMs with structured knowledge retrieved from external knowledge graphs (KGs). However, existing KG-RAG methods either rely on large-scale language models (e.g., ChatGPT) to guide the retrieval process, which leads to high computational costs, or suffer from limited retrieval quality when using lightweight language models, particularly under multi-hop scenarios. We propose LSP-RAG (Latent Scoring Perspectives for Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Knowledge Graphs), a novel KG-RAG framework that enhances hop-wise KG knowledge retrieval through multi-perspective prompted scoring. Each latent scoring perspective is guided by a combination of two types of soft prompts: a perspective-specific soft prompt induces a distinct prompt-conditioned scoring function over candidate triplets, while a contextual soft prompt evolves with each reasoning hop by encoding the query and previously explored KG triplets, enabling the model to preserve consistency and relevance across multi-hop retrieval. Rather than assuming manually defined semantic roles, these latent perspectives are adaptively aggregated to capture heterogeneous relevance signals during retrieval. This design allows LSP-RAG to perform accurate and robust retrieval using lightweight language models. LSP-RAG achieves superior performance across multiple KG-based Question Answering benchmarks compared to existing retrieval systems, including those that rely on much larger language models, demonstrating its effectiveness under limited computational budgets.
☆ FinVeriQA: Financial Research Agents for Question Answering: Routing, Retrieval, MCP Tool Use, and Provenance-Aware Evidence Verification
Meenakshi Rajpurohit, Anna Phan, Ravikumar Komandur Narayanan, Gunanidhi Ramakrishnan, Nathan Howland
Large language models (LLMs) write fluent financial analyses but miscompute ratios, recall stale prices, and route questions to the wrong tool with high confidence. We ask which component should do each job in a financial question-answering assistant, and study it with FinVeriQA, an open-source multi-agent research prototype over SEC filings and live market data: a compact typed-decision model (Laya) routes each question and screens out advice requests, Python computes every number, retrieval and tools fetch evidence, Mistral-7B writes a cited answer, a code validator checks that cited IDs exist and that numbers match computed notes, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposes the pipeline. In live experiments, Laya routed better than Mistral-7B (0.85 vs. 0.52; overall 0.86 vs. 0.68, McNemar p = 0.0003); a 12B Mistral decided no better, and DeepSeek-R1-8B decided better (0.79 vs. 0.68, p = 0.0192) but about 9.9 times more slowly. Mistral-7B computed 29% of 100 financial calculations correctly against 100% for Python, a live quote cut price error from 210% to 0.00%, and hybrid retrieval reached 76% Hit@5 on 50 filing questions. Yet in a live case study, both agent answers passed validation while describing AMD sample data under NVIDIA's and Alphabet's names. A controlled upper-bound study on the FinRank benchmark explains why: when one figure in the shared evidence is corrupted, self-consistency stays confident (agreement 0.55 to 0.59 while accuracy falls from 0.50 to 0.00), and a shared-evidence check (the kind our validator performs) catches 35% of the errors, whereas a check against the original passage catches 77% ($p = 5.96 \times 10^{-8}$); for DeepSeek-R1-8B, 68% vs. 90%. Verification must be independent of the evidence the writer saw.

☆ Can Programs Replace LLM Judges? Executable Program Judges for Scalable and Efficient Relevance Labeling
Eugene Agichtein, Charles L. A. Clarke, Kaustubh Dhole, William Stern
Large language model (LLM) judges have become a common way to create large-scale relevance judgments for retrieval evaluation. However, each judgment requires a potentially expensive call to a frontier model, and the judgments are hard to interpret and may not be reproducible. In this paper, we ask whether an LLM can write a readable program for each topic that replaces its per-document judgments. To address these issues, we propose ExecJudges, a method for generating fast, inspectable and scalable judges for automatic relevance labeling. Specifically, ExecJudges uses a frontier LLM to turn assessment guidelines into executable programs, which rely only on lexical matching, standard NLP libraries like parsers, and pool statistics. An ExecJudges-L variant also uses examples of human labels if available. We evaluate ExecJudges on seven TREC collections by comparing the produced labels with trained NIST assessors, frontier LLM judges, and recently proposed per-topic classifiers. Our results show that ExecJudges agrees with NIST assessors at the level of the Claude Sonnet 5.5 LLM judges on TREC DL 2019-2021. With a small number of human labels per topic, the ExecJudges-L variant agrees with NIST more than per-topic classifiers with the same labels on all seven collections, and either exceeds the agreement of LLM judges provided the same labels or is within about 0.05 of it in Krippendorff's alpha. The labels rank the official TREC DL runs with Kendall's tau of 0.87 to 0.94, and writing the programs incurs a one-time cost of $0.17 to $0.49 per topic, with no additional costs for grading. Our results suggest that ExecJudges offers a reproducible, inspectable, efficient and cost-effective alternative to LLM judges for labeling deep result pools for system evaluation or ranking improvements.
☆ Task-Oriented Network Ranging via Joint Graph and Schedule Design
Zijian Zhang, Yuan Shen
Measuring inter-node distances is the basis for network localization, whereas acquiring node positions does not require a fully connected graph of distances. Existing complete-ranging protocols for network localization require every node pair to exchange signals, which prolongs the ranging cycle. In this paper, we propose sparse signal-multiplexing network ranging (S-SM-NR), a task-oriented framework that adapts the transmit-listen schedule to the ranging task required by network localization. First, we establish the S-SM-NR framework by formulating the joint design of the task graph and the transmit-listen schedule. Then, we analyze the minimum round count required by S-SM-NR and establish a connectivity condition for network localization. Subsequently, we develop a closed-form joint design that constructs the sparse task graph and the balanced transmit-listen schedule. In particular, the joint design can achieve the minimum round count under the complete physical connectivity. Finally, simulations show that the proposed S-SM-NR scheme reduces the occupied-round count and improves the localization accuracy by shortening the ranging cycle.
comment: 16 pages, 14 figures, with appendices
☆ X-split Argus: Learning Reusable History Tokens for Efficient CTR Prediction
Alexander Ploshkin, Nikita Stepanov, Alexey Pismenny, Viacheslav Ovchinnikov, Nikolay Savushkin
Accurate click-through rate (CTR) prediction depends on user representations that capture both persistent preferences and recent intent, yet processing extensive behavioral histories for every ranking request is costly under production compute and latency constraints. We present X-split ARGUS, a framework for ad ranking whose history compressor and online ranker are trained end to end. The compressor encodes past interactions into a compact set of tokens that are computed offline and reused across candidates, while the online ranker scores ads through cross-attention to these tokens and representations of recent events. Training combines an autoregressive loss for click feedback with distillation of candidate-specific click logits from a larger teacher that scores each candidate using the uncompressed history. The number of compressed history tokens and the length of recent history can be adjusted to fit serving compute and latency budgets. Offline evaluation shows a 0.81% relative reduction in normalized entropy (NE) compared with the production baseline. Deployment in a large-scale real-time bidding system increases online inference cost by 15% relative to the production baseline. An online A/B test against this baseline yields relative gains of 4.65% in a business metric reflecting the monetary value of conversions generated for advertisers and 2.96% in clicks.
comment: Alexander Ploshkin, Nikita Stepanov and Alexey Pismenny contributed equally to this work
☆ MARS Technical Report
Tong Liu, Chaoqun Hou, Longxiang Xiong, Junhong Lou, Jiaqi Zheng, Qixin Li, Zixin Zhao, Yong Duan, Xiannian Hu, Fengze Jiang, Yu Zhu, Cheng Guo, Xinyuan Qi, Zi Zhuang, Ping Liu, Lv Shao, Zongwei Wang
Modern industrial recommender systems use multi-stage cascades--retrieval, pre-ranking, ranking, and re-ranking--to narrow millions of candidates to a personalized list. While each stage deploys sophisticated models, pipeline-level decisions on channel activation, quotas, model selection, and score fusion remain engineer-tuned and user-agnostic within each scenario. This report presents MARS (Multi-stage Agentic Recommendation System), extending personalization from individual-stage predictions to full pipeline orchestration. A near-line agent built on fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B generates per-user configurations--a seven-dimensional action covering pipeline mode, retrieval quotas, model selection, fusion weights, and reranker settings--from a constrained action space. Configurations are validated, cached, and consumed asynchronously; the cascade never waits for LLM inference. Schema checks, fallbacks, and a kill switch ensure serving safety. The policy is trained in three stages: Confidence-aware SFT distills schema-valid generation from a teacher model; Format-Anchored Preference Optimization (FAPO) learns action preferences via ActionMask with posterior weighting; Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) refines the policy through Sandbox replay with a frozen reward model, without exposing exploratory actions to live traffic. Two-week A/B tests across five Taobao scenarios with over ten million daily users show positive gains on all key metrics. The largest reach +5.22% V2P and +7.34% GMV, with positive CTR lifts on both click surfaces. About 20% of requests use a lightweight Minimal mode, and deployment shows 12 ms lower mean serving latency versus production.

☆ ReflectRec: Cycle-Consistency Preference Verification for LLM-based Recommendation EMNLP 2026
Dae Kyoo Kim, Heejung Cho, Sungmoo Hong, Eunil Park
CoT-style LLM recommenders generate a natural-language preference note as a chain-of-thought prefix to ranking, but the note is trusted without verification, and the ranker never consults behaviorally similar users. We propose ReflectRec, organized around a preference-to-history round-trip verifier whose recall score serves as an operational signal of preference-to-history recoverability, enabling conditional regeneration for low-recoverability preferences and selection among regeneration attempts. Around this verifier, we wire a semantic Stage-1 prompt, conditional regeneration, and Forward-Look retrieval that injects future watches of behaviorally similar users as a collaborative hint. On MovieLens-100K and MovieLens-1M, the full pipeline outperforms CoT4Rec-ICL by +16.25 / +4.46 pp Hit@10, with positive gains across all ValScore buckets and three LLM backbones (Qwen3-30B, Qwen2.5-72B, and Llama-3.3-70B). We also observe a similar verifier-guided regeneration pattern on Amazon Electronics.

☆ CONCORD-Rec: Catalog-Conditioned Modality Utility for Semantic-ID Diffusion Recommendation
Haopeng Jin, Bingkang Shi, Tao Yu, Yifei Ma, Hao Liu, Hongzhu Yi, Jinwen Luo
Multimodal generative recommendation with discrete semantic identifiers (SIDs) requires distinguishing historical modalities that merely alter token predictions from those that genuinely reduce catalog-level ambiguity. When audiovisual, visual, or textual streams are missing, degraded, or semantically conflicting, uniform fusion and unconstrained token gates can propagate misleading content across iterative denoising steps. We propose CONCORD-Rec, a reliability-conditioned discrete diffusion recommender supervised by counterfactual catalog-partition utility. Given a fixed tokenizer and a partially masked SID state, CONCORD-Rec evaluates out-of-fold teacher coalitions over the exact feasible catalog support and aggregates item posteriors across the target code partition at each unresolved position. Rather than distilling raw token probabilities directly, the resulting counterfactual loss differences supervise an availability-masked tokenwise gate that allocates bounded modality residuals around a behavioral denoiser while retaining an exact behavioral fallback slot. We establish theoretical fixed-support ranking stability bounds under gate perturbations and evaluate position-level and code-conditional allocation across audiovisual and image-text recommendation benchmarks under controlled missingness, signal degradation, and semantic conflict. Across 20 source-compatible protocol-dataset rows, CONCORD-Rec improves NDCG by 4%; under matched 30% conflict it improves NDCG by 14.63%. The full-vs-uniform-T=16 sweep improves quality by 2.00-3.58% while reducing p95 latency by up to 86.89%.
☆ KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch
Zhuo Chen, Jian Wang, Jinjie Gu, Lijun Wu
The growing volume of topically similar papers makes it difficult to identify new work that can offer useful research insights or methodological guidance. We present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight discovery tool that combines multiple sources of evidence into personalized reading priorities. Users specify topics, priorities, exclusions and dates; the system brings together topical relevance, recency, author research histories, collaboration paths and direction-specific institutional context. By exposing each score component and its supporting sources, KnowMe helps readers select promising papers for their current questions and discover relevant work beyond familiar authors. Automatic acquisition, version merging and graph-cache reuse keep this workflow convenient without large language model (LLM) inference during ordinary use. Experiments on 174,640 acquired records show more than threefold faster repeated context preparation, while cached abstracts improve normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 (NDCG@10) from 0.412 to 0.598 on expert-judged retrieval tasks. Complementary analyses examine how the same accumulated records support semantic retrieval, research-history modeling and literature-grounded planning. A browser interface and a structured command-line interface (CLI) make these capabilities available to both researchers and research agents, positioning KnowMe as a practical upstream tool for literature-informed recursive self-improvement (RSI) workflows.

♻ ☆ Toward Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enterprise Retail Workflows over Heterogeneous Data Sources KDD 2027
Jeonghwan Choi, Jibin Hwang, Hayoon Park, Hyeonjae Cheon, Hwanjun Song
Enterprise retail workflows require agents to chain evidence across heterogeneous sources, from structured product and order records to unstructured inquiries and reviews, yet existing agentic RAG benchmarks rarely capture this challenge. To enable controlled evaluation of such workflows, we introduce RetailBridge, a compositional retail benchmark built from persona-driven simulations. Its questions are constructed by linking entities and intermediate answers across heterogeneous sources, requiring agents to identify the relevant sources, carry evidence between them, and produce a grounded answer. To systematically evaluate LLMs on these retail workflows, we develop RetailRAG, a retail-aware framework equipped with auto-schema briefing, source-routed plan chaining, and diagnostic plan revision. RetailRAG consistently outperforms existing agentic RAG baselines across all evaluation axes, serving as a strong reference system for assessing LLM agents on retail workflows. On RetailBridge, evaluating ten LLM backbones with RetailRAG reveals multi-source chaining as the dominant bottleneck across providers and model scales, suggesting that reliable retail agents require explicit cross-source orchestration rather than scaling alone. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/DISL-Lab/RetailBridge.

♻ ☆ UniRank: Benchmarking Ranking Models for Unified Sequential Modeling and Feature Interaction
Honghao Li, Xianquan Wang, Zibin Zhang, Yi Zhang, Kangyi Lin, Yiwen Zhang
Ranking is a core stage in online advertising and recommender systems. Modern ranking models increasingly unify sequential modeling and feature interaction, yet many advances rely on proprietary data, closed implementations, and large-scale industrial infrastructure. This setting limits reproducible comparison and hinders academic study of scaling laws, long-sequence modeling, and multi-task ranking. To address these limitations, this paper proposes UniRank, an open benchmark for ranking models that unify sequential modeling and feature interaction. UniRank uses chronological pointwise autoregressive supervision, standardizes evaluation across feedback tasks, and provides a PyTorch toolkit with Distributed Data Parallel training, operator optimization, mixed-precision training, attention optimization, and other efficiency techniques that reduce hardware requirements. We benchmark 15 representative unified ranking models on five public datasets from short-video, advertising, and e-commerce platforms, with the largest containing over 700 million instances and the longest behavior sequence exceeding $10^5$ interactions. UniRank provides a reproducible foundation for comparing unified ranking models, studying scaling laws under limited compute, and narrowing the gap between academic and industrial ranking research. We believe UniRank benefits researchers, practitioners, and beginners through reproducible experiments, production-oriented evaluation, and accessible implementations. Code and data are available at https://github.com/salmon1802/UniRank.

♻ ☆ Learning Binary Codes with Spiking Neural Networks for Cross-Modal Hashing Retrieval
Yukuan Zhang, Jiarui Zhao, Shangqing Nie, Jin Kuang, Dong Liu, Shengsheng Wang
Cross-modal hashing (CMH) uses compact binary codes for efficient image-text retrieval. Most methods learn image-text relationships in a continuous space and binarize the representation only at the end. Semantic learning and bit decisions thus remain largely separate. This work addresses two key questions concerning hash-bit generation: \textbf{(1) How to determine hash bits?} We leverage the discrete nature of spiking activity and determine each bit through competition between positive and negative spikes accumulated over time, rather than through a single firing event or subsequent thresholding of continuous representations. \textbf{(2) How to generate such hash bits?} We propose an unsupervised spiking framework for cross-modal hashing, in which image and text jointly contribute to hash-bit generation through temporal interaction. An activation constraint further prevents unsupported decisions caused by silent channel pairs. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and support temporal spike competition as a design principle for hash-code generation.
♻ ☆ Recommendation Quality and the Concentration of Consumption: Experimental Evidence from Netflix
Guy Aridor, Winston Chou, Nathan Kallus, Antoine Scheid, Allen Tren, Kevin Zielincki
We study an experiment with 8.5 million users on Netflix's recommender system to measure how improvements in recommendation technology affect the set of products that get consumed. Improvements increase total consumption and users' reliance on recommendations while diffusing recommendations and consumption away from the most popular titles ("superstars") toward a larger number of moderately popular titles ("middle-tail"), with minimal effects on the most niche titles ("long-tail"). Our results challenge the notion that recommender systems polarize consumption -- raising the consumption shares of the head and tail at the expense of the middle -- and suggest that the returns to investing in middle-tail products grow as algorithms improve and platforms scale.
♻ ☆ Explanations that Transfer: Interpreting Medical Retrieval with Sparse AutoEncoders ML4H 2026
Diane Bouchacourt, Gaëtan Brison
Medical AI systems that answer users' queries rely on retrieving medical knowledge from large document collections. In this context, finetuning general models on medical datasets can improve retrieval relevance. Yet the dense embeddings underlying modern retrieval systems remain largely opaque, making it difficult to understand the mechanics behind their results. Moreover, adapting to a specific medical dataset risks losing transferability to new clinical corpora. In this work, we tackle these issues by applying Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to medical information retrieval, transforming dense text embeddings into semantically interpretable representations. To do so, our model combines a reconstruction objective with an InfoNCE contrastive loss that directly preserves query-document relevance. We evaluate three embedding models across six medical retrieval datasets, both in-domain and out-of-domain. Trained on a medical corpus, our sparse codes improve in-domain retrieval over the original embeddings, and lose less out-of-domain performance than their dense counterparts, especially when the target corpus is distant from the training one. Importantly, our experiments show that the method yields interpretable features whose semantic content can be inferred from the queries and documents that activate them most strongly. The interpretation of these features sheds light on why a particular document was retrieved, and transfers beyond the training distribution.

♻ ☆ PEARL: Personalized Streaming Video Understanding with Runtime-Defined Concepts
Yuanhong Zheng, Ruichuan An, Xiaopeng Lin, Yuxing Liu, Sihan Yang, Huanyu Zhang, Haodong Li, Qintong Zhang, Renrui Zhang, Guopeng Li, Yifan Zhang, Yuheng Li, Wentao Zhang
Unlike humans, who learn new concepts from a continuous visual stream, existing personalized vision-language models (VLMs) internalize a predefined concept set during training and operate on static images or offline videos. They cannot register a concept that a user defines in the middle of a stream, nor recall the earlier moments in which it appeared. We formalize this task as Personalized Streaming Video Understanding (PSVU) and introduce PSVU-Bench, the first benchmark for this task, which annotates 132 videos with timestamped questions. Its Concept-Definition, Real-Time and Past-Time QA ask a model to register concepts at arbitrary timestamps, recognize their current state, including user-defined actions, and retrieve their historical evidence. We propose PEARL, a strong plug-and-play baseline that stores user-defined concepts apart from archived video clips and rewrites each query with concept descriptions to retrieve the relevant history. Grounding a named concept in video is a skill shared by all concepts. We therefore construct PSVU-10K, a training set of verified concept questions on public internet videos, and train the retriever and answering VLM of PEARL on it once. Concepts defined at test time still require no training. Applied to three architectures without training, PEARL improves Real-Time QA by 15.05% and Past-Time QA by 12.60% on average over the corresponding offline models, and all three surpass existing online video models on both QA types. Training further improves PEARL on Qwen3-VL-8B by 8.66% on Real-Time QA and 9.39% on Past-Time QA, with gains in every category. Code, data and models are available at https://github.com/Yuanhong-Zheng/PEARL.

♻ ☆ Know Before You Fetch: When Does Confidence-Based Retrieval-Budget Allocation Pay Off?
Zhe Dong, Fang Qin, Manish Shah
Adaptive retrieval-augmented generation uses a signal from the reader, such as its confidence when answering without retrieval (closed-book), to decide whether and how much to retrieve. We compare such methods not with always retrieving many passages but with the best simple policy under the same cap on average passages per query: a fixed depth or a random mixture of fixed depths. Policies allocate zero, one or five passages and are scored on held-out questions. Seven settings of about 2,000 questions combine TriviaQA, Natural Questions and MS MARCO, Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B readers, and two retrieval sources: per-question passage pools and a 3.5-million-passage Wikipedia index. Allocation by confidence could gain in three ways. It rations a scarce budget: at a cap of half a passage per query it beats the best simple policy in all seven settings, by 0.010 to 0.075 in accuracy. It avoids harmful retrieval: at caps of one passage or more, substantial gains appear only on Wikipedia, where passages often overwrite known answers, most robustly for Qwen3-8B on TriviaQA (+0.051, also under exact match and F1). It barely helps to choose depth: closed-book confidence ranks which queries a first passage helps but ranks the choice between one and five passages little better than chance, and with passage pools a fixed depth of two or three passages is as good or better. Once the probe's latency is charged, gains remain only where the gate skips retrieval for most queries; for the larger reader they also depend on the answer metric.

♻ ☆ LLM-Assisted Reranking to Operationalize Nuanced Objectives in Recommender Systems
Amir Ghasemian, Homa Hosseinmardi, Upasana Dutta, Duncan J. Watts
Recommender systems shape what information we see, raising concerns about filter bubbles, radicalization, polarization, and social inequality. Large language models (LLMs) enable more powerful personalization that may intensify these dynamics, yet most recommenders are tuned for engagement or narrow accuracy metrics, with little attention to broader social effects. We investigate whether LLM-assisted reranking, while improving personalization, inadvertently amplifies exposure to ideologically congenial, extreme, or conspiratorial political content, a risk theorized but not yet empirically characterized. Using real YouTube trajectories, we rerank the platform's sidebar candidates by zero-shot prompting across three models, alongside an embedding baseline, and evaluate relevance, ideological alignment and diversity, and exposure to conspiratorial or extremist content. We find that (i) under a pure personalization instruction, reranking improves relevance while narrowing ideological exposure and, on two of three models, promoting problematic content for users with such histories; the third model, which declines most explicitly partisan requests, points to model-specific guardrails; (ii) lightweight prompt-level constraints substantially reduce problematic exposure on all three models, while the regularized rerankers still rank above the platform baseline on relevance; and (iii) synthetic experiments varying topical and partisan cues independently show no fixed preference between them: topic dominates on abortion and immigration, while partisanship takes over on elections, where the topical signal is weaker. Our results highlight the power of LLMs to operationalize contextual nuance in high-stakes political recommendation, and underscore the need to evaluate LLM-assisted personalization beyond accuracy and to treat prompt design as a value-laden choice rather than a neutral default.

☆ Movie2Game-Bench: Holistic Evaluation of Film-to-Game Adaptation Beyond Playability
Jialing Xie, Yifan Zhou, Yiwen Zhang, Junjun He
Adapting a film into a game requires selecting source elements and translating them into player actions, rules, and feedback. We introduce Movie2Game-Bench (M2G-bench), a benchmark for evaluating film-to-game adaptation beyond playability. M2G-bench combines general evaluation, movie-specific evaluation, and playtesting by three GUI model players. The protocol connects source content to gameplay steps and implementation evidence, capturing both content preservation and interactive realization. The benchmark comprises 22 films and 658 source-specific reference items. Evaluating 14 models on the same films with their selected primary harnesses reveals complementary strengths in game quality, adaptation, and player experience. A shared weakness concerns playable sequences: this category has the lowest content-presence mean in all 14 models, averaging 37.9 out of 100 compared with 54.8 for iconic elements. Among judgments of retained emotionaldevelopment content, narrative choices account for 60.0% and scenario operation for 7.2%. These findings identify two linked priorities for film-to-game adaptation: preserving source situations that can support gameplay and connecting retained content to player actions and consequences.
☆ Worth Another Look:Constrained World-Model Planning for Visual Inspection
Ziyue Kang, Zixi Qi, Yuchen Dai, Nana Lv, Xirong Cheng, Liang Liu, Ying Li, Haoyan Wei, Haiyang Yao
Visual inspection in field robotics and environmental monitoring must localize multiple targets under strict compute and sensing caps. Exhaustive sweeps waste calls on absent classes, while myopic and search-free policies stumble over heterogeneous tariff cliffs or discard viewport edits whose value emerges only after re-querying. We formulate inspection over frozen detectors as neuro-symbolic observation planning under partial observability, decoupling a compact recurrent world model (WM) from exact symbolic feasibility and tariff rules. Receding-horizon beam search with online replanning jointly schedules class queries, crops, enhancements, and termination (stop), paired with slack-aware shadow pricing and legal fallback at larger budgets. Across eight terrestrial, optical, and sonar benchmarks, multi-step lookahead outperforms static schedules and search-free offline RL under tight budgets -- gaining up to 28.4 AP percentage points over static priority on RUOD and 15.1 on ARIS -- while dynamic pricing lifts large-budget performance on all eight domains at 11 ms planning cost. Ultimately, pairing lightweight learned dynamics with exact symbolic constraints turns frozen detectors into adaptive, budget-aware inspection agents without retraining.
☆ VideoACE: Benchmarking Agentic Video Understanding through High-Frame-Rate Actions
Luoyuan Zhang, Xuanyu Zheng, Yancheng Long, Haoyang Xu, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao
Agentic video understanding requires models to actively interact with video environments to gather evidence and form judgments. Evaluating this capability therefore requires assessing whether models can translate opportunities for interaction into better understanding. We introduce VideoACE, a benchmark for assessing video understanding under conditions that support sustained interaction. We focus on high-frame-rate action videos, where rapid, subtle changes make targeted observation especially valuable. The benchmark comprises 1,000 multiple-choice questions spanning six categories of fine-grained action understanding, accompanied by temporal evidence annotations and user hints screened for answer leakage. Its evaluation environment combines video inspection tools with a user simulator, allowing models to adjust temporal coverage, sampling density, and spatial detail, and to revisit evidence and revise their judgments under simulated user feedback. We evaluate single-pass observation, autonomous tool use, and tool use combined with user feedback to examine how effectively models exploit these opportunities. Evaluation of five models reveals distinct patterns in how they acquire evidence and respond to opportunities for further interaction. These findings establish VideoACE as a testbed for examining agentic video understanding beyond performance under a fixed observation setting.
☆ Learning Martial Arts Motion Skills for Animating Opponents in VR Sparring Games
Jiqing Wen, Qixuan Shi, Robert LiKamWa, Pavan Turaga
Animating virtual opponents is an important yet challenging task in game development. In martial arts games, opponent motions must not only be physically plausible but also exhibit appropriate technique, timing, transitions, and target-directed intent. Traditional game animations often rely on handcrafted clips, state machine transitions, and procedural adjustments, which can be labor-intensive and may limit the behavioral diversity of non-player characters. This paper presents a martial arts motion skills learning framework for character animation in virtual sparring games. Inspired by Tang Soo Do, we collected a martial arts motion capture dataset containing isolated attacking and defending techniques, technique combinations and transitions, and contextual sparring variations. We first pretrained a reusable repertoire of martial arts motion skills from the captured data using reinforcement learning (RL) with adversarial style rewards, and then adapted these skills with task-specific rewards for target-directed striking and threat-aware evasion. We evaluated the motions generated by the learned policy through a user study, in which participants assessed their physical plausibility, smoothness, and martial arts form. To demonstrate their applicability to interactive gameplay, we developed a VR sparring prototype for Meta Quest headsets. The prototype combines policy-generated motion clips with lightweight state-based control to support interactive opponent behavior. Together, these findings support the feasibility of using a learned martial arts skill repertoire as a motion foundation for animating opponents in VR sparring games.
♻ ☆ Kandinsky 6.0 Video: Foundation Models for Synchronized Video and Audio Generation
Team Kandinsky, Julia Agafonova, Bulat Akhmatov, Mikhail Aksyutin, Grigorii Alekseenko, Anastasia Aliaskina, Olga Androsova, Vladimir Arkhipkin, Anna Averchenkova, Alexander Belykh, Serafima Bocharova, Sofiya Bogakovskaya, Anton Bukashkin, Mark Bulygin, Kirill Buzygin, Irina Cheremnykh, Kirill Chernyshev, Mikhail Chernyshov, Vladimir Chernyy, David Chikovani, Georgy Daniltsev, Denis Dimitrov, Anna Dmitrienko, Vladimir Dokholyan, Sergey Emelyanov, Dmitry Ermilov, Georgii Fedorov, Polina Gavrilova, Nikolai Gerasimenko, Aleksandr Gordeev, Andrey Inozemtsev, Andrei Ivaniuta, Alexander Ivanov, Mikhail Karaev, Anastasiia Kargapoltseva, Ivan Kirillov, Nikita Kiselev, Valeria Kobenko, Yury Kolabushin, Denis Koposov, Anatoly Korobov, Vladimir Korviakov, Maria Kovaleva, Kirill Kozlov, Denis Krzhivokolskiy, Konstantin Kuklev, Alexander Kunitsyn, Sergey Kuzin, Vladislav Lakhtionov, Alexey Letunovskiy, Maxim Litvinov, Alexander Lyulkov, Georgy Makarov, Kirill Malakhov, Egor Malykh, Mikhail Mamaev, Dmitrii Mikhailov, Polina Mikhailova, Ivan Mikheev, Elizaveta Muromtseva, Nikolai Nazarkin, Tatiana Nikulina, Lev Novitskiy, Stanislav Onuchin, Nikita Osterov, Denis Parkhomenko, Anatoliy Parpara, Vladimir Polovnikov, Konstantin Reznikov, Azat Saginbaev, Nikita Samsonov, Alexander Sentsov, Nikita Shaimov, Artem Sherstyuk, Andrey Shutkin, Egor Silvestrov, Bulat Suleimanov, Matvey Suprunov, Sergey Taranov, Irina Tolstykh, Tatiana Trofimuk, Ilya Trushkin, Aleksandra Tsybina, Olga Varlashina, Viacheslav Vasilev, Ilya Vasiliev, Eugeny Vilisov, Sergey Yakubson, Konstantin Zakharov
We present Kandinsky 6.0 Video, a family of foundation diffusion models for synchronized text-to-audio-video generation, comprising Kandinsky 6.0 Video Lite (3B parameters) and Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro (29B parameters). Both models generate 5-second video clips with synchronized 44 kHz audio, including lip-sync, in text-to-audio-video (T2AV) and image-to-audio-video (I2AV) modes; a built-in super-resolution model raises the output resolution to Full-HD (1920x1080). Building on the video generation capabilities of Kandinsky 5.0, Kandinsky 6.0 Video employs a dual-stream CrossDiT architecture that connects a pretrained video stream and a newly trained audio stream through bidirectional cross-attention for temporal and semantic alignment. Our continuous pretraining strategy first trains the audio stream from scratch on large-scale audio corpora and then trains both streams jointly on paired audio-video data while preserving unimodal fidelity; pretraining is followed by supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement-learning-based post-training, and distillation. In side-by-side human evaluation, Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro clearly outperforms its predecessor, Kandinsky 5.0 Video Pro, and remains competitive with leading audio-video generation models, outperforming LTX 2.5 and Seedance 2.0 in speech quality. To accelerate open research and deployment in multimedia generation, we release the code, model checkpoints, and diffusers integration under the MIT license.

♻ ☆ Facial Action Unit Detection Based on Multi-task Learning Strategy for Unlabeled Facial Images in the Wild
Ziqiao Shang, Bin Liu
Facial Action Unit (AU) detection often relies on highly-cost accurate labeling or inaccurate pseudo labeling techniques in recent years. How to introduce large amounts of unlabeled facial images in the wild into supervised AU detection frameworks has become a challenging problem. Additionally, nearly every type of AUs has the problem of unbalanced positive and negative samples. Inspired by other multi-task learning frameworks, we first propose a multi-task learning strategy boosting AU detection in the wild through jointing facial landmark detection and AU domain separation and reconstruction. Our introduced dual domains facial landmark detection framework can solve the lack of accurate facial landmark coordinates during the AU domain separation and reconstruction training process, while the parameters of homostructural facial extraction modules from these two similar facial tasks are shared. Moreover, we propose a pixel-level feature alignment scheme to maintain the consistency of features obtained from two separation and reconstruction processes. Furthermore, a weighted asymmetric loss is proposed to change the contribution of positive and negative samples of each type of AUs to model parameters updating. Experimental results on three widely used benchmarks demonstrate our superiority to most state-of-the-art methods for AU detection.
♻ ☆ Auditing Hyperstimulation at Scale in Child-Facing YouTube Videos
Shao-Yu Chu, Qiyu Li, Xuan Liu, Shuang Hao, Haojian Jin
Parents, pediatricians, and journalists have raised concern that child-facing videos are becoming increasingly stimulating (faster-paced, louder, and more visually dense), but this concern rests mostly on ad hoc observation rather than systematic measurement. We present a large-scale audit of hyperstimulation patterns, which we refer to as content-independent production choices, such as rapid cutting, that may place demands on children's developing cognitive and sensory processing capacities. Drawing on parents' Reddit discussions and developmental psychology, we develop computational metrics for 12 hyperstimulation patterns. We apply these metrics to 16,375 videos from 542 child-facing YouTube channels spanning 2015-2026. We found broad increases in stimulation over time, with cut rates rising across all five content categories. Nearly a quarter of the channels increased in at least one stimulation pattern over time. More stimulating videos also tended to receive more views, but the relevant stimulation patterns differed across content types.
♻ ☆ FLARE: Full-Modality Long-Video Audiovisual Retrieval Benchmark with User-Simulated Queries NeurIPS 2026
Qijie You, Hao Liang, Mingrui Chen, Bohan Zeng, Meiyi Qiang, Zhenhao Wong, Wentao Zhang
As video becomes increasingly central to information dissemination and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) continue to advance, evaluating video retrieval has become increasingly important. In realistic search scenarios, this requires matching short user queries to long-form content using both visual and auditory evidence. Yet existing retrieval benchmarks are still dominated by short clips, single modalities, and caption-based evaluation. We introduce FLARE, a full-modality long-video audiovisual retrieval benchmark with user-simulated queries. Built from 399 carefully screened Video-MME videos (10--60 min, 225.4 h) to ensure source quality and diversity, FLARE contains 87,697 clips annotated with vision, audio, and unified audiovisual captions, together with 274,933 user-style queries. Cross-modal queries are further filtered by a hard bimodal constraint, requiring retrieval to fail under either modality alone but succeed when both are combined. FLARE evaluates models under two regimes, caption-based and query-based retrieval, across vision, audio, and unified audiovisual settings. Experiments with 15 representative retrievers show that user-style queries substantially change model behavior, strong caption-based performance does not always transfer to query-based retrieval, and audio--language alignment remains a key bottleneck for unified audiovisual retrieval. Our code and data are released at https://flarebench.github.io/

♻ ☆ Lifting 3D Gaussians: A Wavelet Multiresolution Representation for Scalable Gaussian Splatting Streaming
Yuang Shi, Géraldine Morin, Simone Gasparini, Wei Tsang Ooi
3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) represents a scene as an unstructured set of primitives optimized at a single scale, offering no native support for progressive delivery to heterogeneous devices. Existing scalable approaches organize these primitives into independent quality layers or spatial hierarchies. However, maintaining separate splat representations across scales introduces redundancy, while independent layers have limited ability to correct coarse geometry as finer detail arrives. We present LiftGS, a multiresolution representation that organizes a scene into a coarse Gaussian set and a tree of refinements. Each refinement replaces one coarse Gaussian with two finer children whose attributes are learned relative to their parent. Inspired by wavelet lifting, we encode these changes using a shared detail vector and per-attribute factors that allow the two children to differ asymmetrically from the parent. A client first receives the coarse set, then reconstructs and substitutes children as refinement data arrives. This construction reuses previously transmitted attributes to encode finer detail and removes replaced parents from the active rendering set, reducing both refinement payload and rendering memory. Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets show LiftGS cuts splat redundancy from over 65% to under 25%, reduces transmission payload and GPU memory by up to 2.4x and 5.5x over state-of-the-art scalable-3DGS baselines, achieves smooth quality transitions in simulated progressive delivery, and compresses a further 8.7x with standard coding at negligible quality loss. Project website: https://yuang-ian.github.io/liftgs/

☆ VIBRA: Backward-Compatible Cross-Modal Retrieval with Consensus Barycenters
Shubing Yang, Xutong Liu, Dongfang Zhao
Backward-compatible retrieval enables a new encoder to query the gallery that an old model has already encoded, so that a cross-modal retrieval system can be upgraded without re-encoding billions of items. Existing compatible methods either fit the old query and stay near the accuracy of the old model, or run the old and the new encoder for every query. We propose VIBRA, which matches relevance on the old gallery, corrects the errors of a single model with the barycenter of several views, which is itself a query in the old space, and trains the new encoder to inherit this consensus, so that models absent at deployment still shape every query. We show that the barycenter gains margin over the average of its views exactly when their hardest irrelevant items differ, and we characterize the share of this gain that one encoder can reach. On five benchmarks with five upgrades among six CLIP, MetaCLIP and SigLIP2 backbones, VIBRA is the best compatible method in all 50 settings, improving Recall@1 by up to 5.6 points over the strongest baseline and by up to 18.0 points over the old model, while adding less than 1 ms to the latency of the new encoder.

The pool turned out to be sortable by document length alone, which makes precision-style metrics on it uninformative; regenerating it under a shared length budget removes that shortcut and leaves the reading-depth result standing. The four-level agreement score such systems report, ours included, is a binary probability cut at fixed thresholds, so it follows the classifier's confidence rather than its ranking and falls as labels accumulate. And uncertainty sampling, the obvious way to implement a "suggest the next CV" button, leaves model quality intact but raises the committee's total reading load above the no-label baseline, because the CVs it asks about are the ones that would otherwise be skipped. A fourth result shows where to look next: a hosted LLM embedding model lifts zero-label ordinal discrimination from 0.66 to 0.80 under length control, then stops mattering once the session model has two dozen labels; a local cross-encoder matches that cold-start gain without sending data out. The root cause is that only one next item is logged per user, so RL treats every other candidate as wrong. Yet these candidates are the model's most plausible alternatives, and often the next items of other users with similar histories. Penalising them pushes down exactly what similar users choose next, and these items drop out of those users' candidate lists. This diagnosis points directly to a remedy: out-of-rollout anchoring, a single additional loss term that preserves the SFT model's ordering of the items outside the rollout. It keeps the gain at the top and restores recall to the SFT level on all five datasets, and it is effective under other RL configurations as well. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of this recall loss: we measure it, identify its cause, and show that, once the cause is known, a simple remedy suffices.

Some generative recommenders, including the Uber Eats search engine we are building, write a whole results page, stores with their menu items, in one decoding pass. Every Semantic ID on such a page must name a real store or item that is eligible for the search, such as a store that delivers to the user's location, and that is not already on the page. Each item must also belong to the store above it. A trie over the catalog keeps identifiers real, but eligibility and repetition change with every request and token, and the grammar-constrained decoder we tried could not enforce these changing rules exactly and quickly. We call this constraint LEGIT, for live eligibility gating over identifier tries. Numbering trie leaves depth first turns each rule into a range lookup over one store trie and one item trie, and every generated page passes an independent catalog check. Our fastest implementation walks the trie on the CPU while the GPU runs the model, needs no custom kernel, and cuts time per output token by 65.9 percent against the direct GPU implementation, to about 1.7 times the unconstrained cost. ♻ ☆ RecHarness: A Bandit-Routed Agentic Harness for Self-Evolving Recommender Systems
Haoran Ling, Yuecheng Li, Zeyu Song, Jing Yao, Shuwen Kang, Songcheng Ren, Chi Lu, Wenjin Wu, Peng Jiang
Optimizing recommender models remains heavily reliant on manual iteration over architectures, objectives, and training strategies. While LLM-based agents can automate this trial-and-error process, relying on LLMs to both select modification directions and formulate concrete hypotheses can lead to unstable search under limited trial budgets. Inspired by the above challenge, we propose RecHarness, a Bandit-Routed Agentic Harness for automated recommender model optimization. RecHarness decouples the optimization process into two steps: a bandit router selects the next modification direction according to historical validation feedback, while the LLM generates a concrete optimization hypothesis and executable code edit within the selected direction. To sustain long-horizon exploration, RecHarness uses a jump-basin mechanism to activate a structural-jump arm when local edits stagnate. Across multiple recommendation tasks, datasets, and model backbones, RecHarness achieves more consistent performance improvements and uses limited trial budgets more effectively than LLM-directed search. During a 7-day online A/B test on a large-scale short-video advertising platform, the selected candidate improves ADVV by 2.084%, Revenue by 0.534%, and Exposure by 0.559%. Code is available at: https://github.com/6lyc/RecHarness.
comment: 17 pages, 3 figures
♻ ☆ REGER: Modeling inter-item Relations with Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
Yuxi Huang, Silin Zhou, Chenhao Wang, Zihan Li, Gangming Guo, Pei Ke, Lisi Chen, Shen Gao, Shuo Shang
Personalized recommendation depends on learning semantic and collaborative relations among items from online content and user interactions. Generative recommendation (GR) offers a promising paradigm by autoregressively generating discrete semantic IDs (SIDs) of items. However, randomly initialized SID token embeddings and GR models trained from scratch do not directly inherit the semantic relations inherent in items, while inter-item collaborative relations are learned largely implicitly through token-level attention and next-token supervision. To address this limitation, we propose REGER, a unified framework that explicitly incorporates inter-item relations into semantic pretraining, history encoding, and SID generation. We pretrain the GR model through generative semantic retrieval, enabling it to inherit inter-item semantic similarity by learning to generate semantic neighbors' SIDs. We combine global attention with local attention aligned with SID boundaries to capture historical context and directed transitions between adjacent items. We formalize item-level preference distillation on the SID prefix tree, deriving an exact factorization of item preference distributions into prefix conditionals and a weighted decomposition of item-level KL divergence into conditional KL terms. Guided by this decomposition, we renormalize the generator's probabilities over legal next tokens and match the resulting distributions to the teacher's conditional preferences along the ground-truth SID path, jointly optimizing the distillation objective with cross-entropy. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed preference distillation and demonstrate that REGER consistently outperforms existing GR baselines while retaining efficient inference.
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures
♻ ☆ EE-Motion: An EEG-based Web Architecture for Live Affective Music Recommendation
Sabino Roccotelli, Potito Aghilar, Vito Walter Anelli, Alejandro Bellogín, Tommaso Colafiglio, Michelantonio Trizio, Tommaso Di Noia
Music listening is intrinsically tied to emotion, which drifts continuously within a single session. Although modern browsers interface with wearable brain-computer interfaces, recommendation systems remain structured around discrete logs and lack the infrastructure to integrate continuous physiological signals. Furthermore, existing affect-aware models rely on static user profiles and offline training, failing to serve anonymous newcomers without model retraining. We present a web platform that resolves both challenges. Pairing with a consumer electroencephalogram (EEG) headband over Web Bluetooth, the system captures live EEG, mapping frontal alpha asymmetry and arousal index to normalized valence-arousal proxy coordinates on Russell's circumplex plane. Driven by these coordinates, an affective adapter unifies structurally diverse recommendation backbones under a shared live scoring mechanism. By parameterizing anonymous visitors through a few favorite tracks, the module recommends tracks conditioned on live proxy coordinates. This demonstrates that real-time EEG-derived control signals can steer recommendations without persistent user tables or model retraining.
♻ ☆ Enhancing Stock Market Information Retrieval with Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Huan Phong Thai, Thu Anh Ngoc Le, Nhu Huynh Thi Le, Nhan Huu Tran, Lenh Cong Phan Pham, Hong Nhung Nguyen
Natural Language Processing (NLP) has been widely applied in financial domains, enabling automated analysis and retrieval of stock market information. However, traditional NLP-based systems often struggle with maintaining contextual accuracy and generating relevant responses in dynamic financial environments. To address these challenges, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models have emerged as a powerful solution, combining retrieval-based methods with generative capabilities to enhance response quality. In this study, we present a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system designed to generate responses related to stock market information. The system integrates retrieval-based and generative approaches to enhance the accuracy and relevance of financial text generation. To evaluate its effectiveness, we employ the ROUGE metric, specifically ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L, to measure lexical and structural similarity between generated and reference texts. Experimental results on a dataset of 100 stock market-related queries demonstrate high ROUGE scores, indicating strong alignment with reference documents. Additionally, we assess latency to evaluate the system responsiveness, achieving an average response time of 1.16 seconds. These findings confirm that our RAG model is capable of providing accurate and timely stock market insights, making it a promising approach for financial information retrieval.

♻ ☆ CodeHID: Learning an Addressable Hierarchical Code Index for Generative Code Retrieval WSDM'27
Zhen Li, Yuhong Chen, Wenhao Xu, Xiaodong Li, Hui Li
Code retrieval models have predominantly relied on a flat matching paradigm that treats code snippets as independent candidates, making them less capable of distinguishing similar code candidates. Generative retrieval offers a solution by constructing a learnable index over the code corpus, guiding the retriever to better understand how code candidates are semantically organized and addressed. However, naively applying generative retrieval in the code retrieval task may result in operating over an identifier space whose prefixes do not correspond to meaningful code-semantic regions. In this paper, we propose CodeHID, a generative code retrieval framework that reformulates the code retrieval task from flat candidate matching to coarse-to-fine semantic address generation. CodeHID relies on two core components. First, Pseudo-Neighbor Guided DocID Learning constructs a globally static hierarchical index by applying multi-level residual quantization and $k$-nearest-neighbor pseudo-supervision, ensuring that semantically related code snippets share prefixes while preserving target-level separability. Second, Dual-Phase DocID Generation Guidance reliably navigates this fixed index by combining training-side ranking enhancements, using hard negatives and rank distillation, with inference-side candidate constraints and prefix-aware decoding. Extensive experiments on CoSQA and ProCQA benchmarks demonstrate that CodeHID outperforms existing sparse retrieval, pre-trained code models, dense code retrieval, and generative retrieval baselines by a large margin in most cases, achieving particularly strong improvements in rank-one retrieval metrics.

♻ ☆ Beyond Retrieval: Learning Compact User Representations for Scalable LLM Personalization EMNLP 2026
Heng Cao, Fan Zhang, Jian Yao, Yujie Zheng, Changlin Zhao, Lu Hao, Yuxuan Wei, Wangze Ni, Huaiyu Fu, Yuqian Sun, Xuyan Mo
Personalizing large language models requires adapting model behavior to individual users while preserving robustness and deployment-scale efficiency. Existing approaches typically personalize LLMs either at the input level, by retrieving user histories or constructing profile prompts, or at the parameter level, by maintaining user-specific parameter-efficient modules. The former makes personalization sensitive to retrieval quality and prompt design, whereas the latter incurs storage and maintenance costs that grow with the user population. To address these limitations, we propose TAP-PER (Temporal Attentive Prefix for PERsonalization), a prefix-based framework that encodes user preferences as learnable representations, avoiding the serialization of user histories into prompts and replacing heavy per-user adapters with lightweight user-state prefix embeddings. Inspired by personalized recommendation systems, TAP-PER decomposes user modeling into user-state and query-conditioned components, and incorporates temporal signals to capture the evolving nature of user interests. Experiments on six LaMP tasks show that TAP-PER consistently outperforms prompt-based and model-based baselines across classification, rating, and generation settings. Moreover, TAP-PER uses 130x fewer per-user parameters than OPPU and roughly half the total parameter footprint of PER-PCS at the 1,000-user scale, demonstrating scalable personalization without prompt-serialized histories or heavy per-user adapters.
comment: EMNLP 2026 Findings
♻ ☆ Efficient Generative Retrieval for E-commerce Search with Semantic Cluster IDs and Expert-Guided RL
Jianbo Zhu, Xing Fang, Jing Wang, Mingmin Jin, Bokang Wang, Guangxin Song, Zhenyu Xie, Junjie Bai
Generative retrieval offers a promising alternative by unifying the fragmented multi-stage retrieval process into a single end-to-end model. However, its practical adoption in industrial e-commerce search remains challenging, given the massive and dynamic product catalogs, strict latency requirements, and the need to align retrieval with downstream ranking goals. In this work, we propose a retrieval framework tailored for real-world recall scenarios, positioning generative retrieval as a recall-stage supplement rather than an end-to-end replacement. Our method, CQ-SID (Category-and-Query constrained Semantic ID), employs category-aware and query-item contrastive learning along with Residual Quantized VAEs to encode items into hierarchical semantic cluster identifiers, significantly reducing beam search complexity. Additionally, we develop EG-GRPO (Expert-Guided Group Relative Policy Optimization), a reinforcement learning approach that aligns generative recall with downstream ranking under sparse rewards by injecting ground-truth samples to stabilize training. Offline experiments on TmallAPP search logs show that CQ-SID achieves up to 26.76% and 11.11% relative gains in semantic and personalized click hitrate over RQ-VAE baselines, while halving beam search size. EG-GRPO further improves multi-objective performance. Online A/B tests confirm gains in GMV (+1.15%) and UCTCVR (+0.40%). The generative recall channel now contributes substantially in production, accounting for over 50.25% of exposures, 58.96% of clicks, and 72.63% of purchases, demonstrating a viable path for deploying generative retrieval in real-world e-commerce systems.
♻ ☆ Retrieving Complementary Evidence for Multi-Hop RAG with Semantic Gain Graphs
Zeliang Li, Xiaofen Xing, Kailing Guo, Xiangmin Xu
Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) requires finding documents whose evidence is useful in combination. Query relevance and graph connectivity help locate related content, but neither directly measures the additional information one document contributes given another. We introduce SG$^2$RAG, a framework that represents this complementarity through semantic gain. Offline, a large language model assesses the relevant and nonredundant information contributed by one chunk given another within neighborhoods proposed by semantic similarity. These ordered assessments are aggregated into symmetric edge weights to construct a reusable Semantic Gain Graph. Online, controlled Personalized PageRank starts from query-relevant seeds and ranks complementary evidence beyond the initial retrieval set. Experiments on MuSiQue, 2Wiki, and HotpotQA with two language model backbones show that SG$^2$RAG achieves the best average EM, F1, and Recall@10 among the evaluated single-retrieval methods. Under identical candidate support and propagation, semantic gain improves average F1 and Recall@10 over similarity weighting by 4.08 and 4.31 points. Analyses of supporting documents and improvements in three iterative retrieval frameworks further support its effectiveness as a reusable retrieval component.

☆ CodeReel: Accelerating Code-to-Video Agents with Exact Frame Reuse and Blocking-Aware Scheduling
Junyi Shen, Yao Lu
Coding agents make videos by writing and refining programs in a build--inspect--edit loop. A finished film costs a median of $2.85 in model calls and 11 minutes, over a third of that time in builds that block the agent. We find that much of this time is avoidable, for two reasons. First, 37.5% of the frames of a session's later films were drawn before, many shifted in time or inside an edited scene. Second, half of the builds stop at a check, where the agent needs only the verdict, but which builds stop is unknown until the checks finish. We present CodeReel, a training-free execution layer behind agents' existing commands. Exact frame reuse keys each frame by its drawing commands, regardless of its position in time, and reuses each frame whose key recurs. Blocking-aware scheduling runs the checks first and starts the render alongside them, at idle priority, unless the session's recent builds make a pass unlikely. Scheduling spends CPU to answer sooner and reuse returns it; exact keys let later versions use frames rendered for a failed one as the agent thinks. We introduce EditLoop, a benchmark of replayable agent sessions whose films are checked against renders from scratch. On it, CodeReel cuts the agent's wait by 36.3% against Rebuild, a warm pipeline with parallel rendering, and by 57.9% against Sequential, today's step-by-step pipeline. On time-shifting edits its reuse renders 43.9%, close to the 43.0% whose pixels are new, while Manim-style caching renders 99.8%. With real agents, the median wait per build is 0.62x Rebuild's in Claude Code, on topics never used in development, and 0.67x in Codex CLI. The gain holds for five models and two frameworks.

☆ Streaming Generative Video Compression with Embedding Alignment and In-Context Propagation
Zhitao Wang, Hengyu Man, Han Liu, Wenrui Li, Debin Zhao, Xiaopeng Fan
Video compression at ultra-low bitrates presents substantial challenges in preserving perceptual quality. Although pretrained video diffusion transformers (DiTs) provide powerful generative priors, existing generative video compression (GVC) methods built on them typically rely on computationally expensive VAE decoders to reconstruct video frames. Moreover, jointly refining multiple frames to exploit the inherent spatiotemporal modeling capabilities of video DiTs introduces additional buffering delay. To address these challenges, we propose SGVC, a streaming generative video compression framework that adapts a pretrained latent video DiT into a causal pixel-space refiner. Specifically, SGVC projects decoded features from a contextual pixel codec directly into the DiT input embedding space. To bridge the representation gap between codec-derived embeddings and pretrained DiT embeddings, we introduce Embedding Alignment, which aligns the projected embeddings with input embeddings extracted from the original frames during training. The refined DiT hidden states are then mapped directly to the pixel domain through a lightweight reconstruction path, bypassing the pretrained VAE decoder. To further exploit the spatiotemporal priors of the video DiT while maintaining causal decoding, we introduce In-Context Propagation, which reuses layer-wise K/V states across frames to exploit historical generative context, improving temporal consistency without requiring clip-wise buffering. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SGVC achieves competitive rate-perception performance, with average BD-rate savings of 71.97% over S$^2$VC in terms of DISTS. Project Page: https://chigland.github.io/SGVC/

☆ LeViT-UNet++: Towards Balanced Fine-Grained Details and Context for Efficient Medical Image Segmentation
Guoping Xu, Jinling Zhu, Liuyue Li
Efficient medical image segmentation is essential for clinical applications requiring fast and accurate delineation, such as surgical navigation, radiation therapy, and real-time image-guided intervention. Despite substantial advances in convolutional neural networks and Transformers, attaining high accuracy under limited computational resources remains difficult, because reducing model complexity often sacrifices fine-grained structural details and global context modeling, yielding an unfavorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off. To address this, we propose LeViT-UNet++, an efficient encoder-decoder architecture that better balances local detail preservation and global context modeling. Specifically, we introduce a Haar Wavelet Multi-Scale Downsampling (HWMD) module that decomposes feature representations into low- and high-frequency components to extract multi-scale structural information, thereby mitigating detail loss during downsampling. We further develop a depthwise convolution-based decoder that integrates multi-scale global representations from Transformer blocks with local spatial features, enabling progressive feature refinement while reducing computational overhead. Evaluated on four benchmarks (Synapse, ACDC, LA2018, and MSD Heart) under both 2D and 3D settings, LeViT-UNet++ achieves competitive accuracy with a compact parameter footprint and fast inference. On Synapse, for instance, it attains a DSC of 76.57% with only 8.025M parameters and 241.72 FPS, confirming a favorable accuracy-efficiency balance. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining wavelet-based multi-scale feature extraction with lightweight local-global feature fusion for efficient medical segmentation. The source code is available at https://github.com/apple1986/levit_unet_pp.

♻ ☆ Words Speak Louder? Exploring the Language Shortcut of LLM-Driven Incomplete Multimodal Learning
Qiangchang Wang, Chong Xiao, Xiaokun Bai, Rundong He, Zhuang Qi, Xusheng Liang, Zhibin Wu, Wenhao Li
Is a face or a voice still heard once the words are known? Incomplete multimodal learning increasingly uses large language models (LLMs) as fusion engines: modality features enter as token blocks and missing modalities become placeholders. We find that LLM-driven fusion can override non-verbal evidence it can read. Contrasting its full-input prediction with counterfactual views, the same model shown one modality or no content, we identify language shortcuts. We build MR-Bench: MR-Bench-A types every test sample of four sentiment benchmarks; MR-Bench-H contains 900 human-validated clips (620 language-shortcut, LS; 280 non-verbal-shortcut, NS) from seven sources, and every model is scored on all of them. Zero-shot MLLMs solve at most 32.7% of the LS clips; adding the transcript to the muted video lowers vision-language accuracy by 46.1-53.1 points. Yet inverting a text-only model's answers solves 94.4%, so LS accuracy alone cannot establish use of non-verbal evidence. Inside the fusion LLM, fused states align increasingly with the text view late in the decoder. Counterfactual-View Reliability learning (CoVeR) trains views as unimodal judges and withholds fused supervision where they disagree. It achieves state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks without extra inference cost in accuracy mode. On MR-Bench-H, it reaches 61.7% LS and 93.6% NS accuracy; robust mode raises LS accuracy to 63.0% while lowering NS accuracy to 84.8%. Among LS clips solved without text, adding text causes errors on 30.1% with CoVeR versus 32.2% with LLM-Fusion. Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/CoVeR/.

♻ ★ DAT: Dual-Aware Adaptive Transmission with Small-Large Model Collaboration for Edge-Cloud Anomaly Detection AAAI 2027
Qi Guo, Zheming Yang, Yunqing Hu, Chang Zhao, Wen Ji
Continuous video anomaly detection is critical for timely safety monitoring in edge--cloud visual systems, but it remains challenging because abnormal events are sparse, transient, and require both low-latency anomaly detection and verifiable visual evidence. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer strong semantic understanding and visual reasoning capabilities for such event-centric analysis, yet applying them to continuous video streams incurs prohibitive computation and communication overhead under bandwidth-constrained edge--cloud deployments. To address this challenge, we propose DAT, a dual-aware adaptive transmission framework that supports high-quality semantic generation, low-latency anomaly detection, and progressive visual evidence supplementation. DAT first uses a collaborative small--large model cascade, where a lightweight edge-side model filters non-target-event frames, performs object detection, and triggers MLLM inference only for suspicious frames. Building on this cascade, DAT introduces visual guidance and semantic prompting to improve structured event understanding, localization, and output consistency. It further schedules semantic anomaly alarms and visual evidence through a semantic- and bandwidth-aware multi-stream transmission optimization method. Experimental results show that DAT achieves 97.77\% F1 in traffic-accident detection while substantially reducing inference and communication overhead. On continuous video workloads, DAT lowers the MLLM call rate to 13.71\% and reduces upload volume by at least 95.72\% compared with representative edge--cloud baselines. Under severe congestion, DAT reduces weighted alarm delay by up to 87.9\%, demonstrating efficient MLLM-based anomaly detection under constrained edge--cloud networks.
